blocks.text: In June 2000 the Treasury published a working paper by Suzi Kerr and Jason Timmins titled Economic Geography & Spatial Statistics: Theory and Empirics of New Zealand Regions. It examined regional economic characteristics and used GIS as part of the analytical method. Critchlow Associates supplied Census96 data, including geographic boundaries and demographic, household, labour-force and socioeconomic information organised at meshblock, area-unit, territorial-authority and regional-council levels. The paper also refers to ArcView software, but this does not establish that Critchlow was an ArcView distributor.

blocks.text: The researchers used statistical geography prepared by Statistics New Zealand, whose work is described in Chapter 16. With packaged data and desktop software, they could examine regional differences without establishing the kind of GIS production system used by mapping agencies in the previous decade.

blocks.text: The geographic units gave the researchers several scales at which to examine the same country. Meshblocks provided fine-grained population geography, while area units and local-government boundaries supported broader regional comparison. Economic variables could be mapped rather than read only as columns in national tables. GIS made geographic pattern easier to inspect and allowed analysis to be organised around places rather than one national average, while causal interpretation still depended on the underlying evidence.

blocks.text: The project also shows how government GIS drew on organisations outside the department. The paper says Critchlow Associates supplied both Census96 data and ArcView software, but other evidence identifies Critchlow as a MapInfo supplier and Eagle Technology as Esri's New Zealand distributor. The paper's wording does not establish Critchlow as an ArcView reseller, and the precise software-supply arrangement is unclear. Statistics New Zealand remained the source of the census and statistical geography, while Critchlow packaged data for desktop analysis. Policy researchers could combine national data, commercially prepared spatial information and GIS tools without producing every component themselves.

blocks.text: By 2000 this kind of use required far less technical infrastructure than it would have a decade earlier. An analyst could work with regional boundaries and attributes on a desktop computer rather than submit a mapping request to a specialist production unit. The work was still recognisably GIS, but the organisational role had changed. Geography had become another analytical dimension available to a policy team.
